CASE 1 — REDWOOD RETAIL

Redwood has connected its Sentinel workspace to the Defender portal. Its firewall emits correctly formatted CEF through local4 at informational severity to a supported Linux forwarder. The forwarder receives the messages, but its DCR currently collects local5 at error and above.

The SOC wants a scheduled detector evaluated every five minutes. The source can arrive 20 minutes late; the approved design is a 45-minute event-time lookback. Matching alerts must include the source IP as an entity. The SOC also wants matching new high-severity incidents assigned and tagged without calling an external service.

A tier-one analyst may assign and close incidents but may not edit analytics rules. A separate engineer owns detection configuration. The SOC must validate data collection and representative detection results before declaring coverage. Assume supported connectors and required licensing are available.
questions.takeaway: Responder supports incident management without the detection-editing authority of Contributor.

title: MITRE coverage, anomalies, and multistage correlation
subtitle: Measure useful coverage and tune behavioral findings without treating unusual as malicious.
intro: MITRE ATT&CK gives a shared vocabulary for attacker goals and techniques, helping the SOC compare detections against relevant attack paths. A colored matrix cell is a planning signal, not proof that an attack will be stopped. Behavioral anomalies add evidence that activity differs from a baseline, while correlation can connect weak signals into a stronger incident. SC-200 tests these distinctions and the engineering steps needed to improve coverage. Current Sentinel onboarding to the Defender portal also changes the correlation engine: Fusion is disabled for those workspaces and its function is replaced by Defender XDR correlation. Recognize that transition when reading older labs.

sections.title: Read the coverage matrix critically
sections.body: A tactic describes an attacker’s objective, such as credential access or lateral movement. A technique describes how the attacker pursues it. Sentinel’s MITRE view can show existing active detection coverage and available content associated with these categories. Use the distinction between enabled rules and available templates to identify a real gap. A template without its required source is not operational protection. Validate the rule’s actual query, scope, data quality, and expected evidence. Prioritize techniques relevant to your assets and threat model rather than enabling every template simply to fill the entire matrix with color.

sections.title: Understand what an anomaly claims
sections.body: An anomaly is a departure from an established pattern. It can be useful context for hunting and correlation, but unusual does not automatically mean malicious. Sentinel includes UEBA-oriented and machine-learning anomaly approaches that analyze different aspects of behavior. Results in Anomalies include rule information and reasons that should guide interpretation. Check the relevant rule’s data requirements and baseline assumptions before using an anomaly as evidence. A backup job, new application rollout, or legitimate administrative change may produce unusual activity, so compare the finding with business context and other identity, network, or endpoint evidence.

sections.title: Tune custom anomalies through a controlled comparison
sections.body: Built-in anomaly configurations are not edited like an ordinary custom KQL rule. Duplicate the supported anomaly rule, change the allowed parameters or threshold in the customized copy, and assess its results in Flighting mode. Compare findings in Anomalies using the template and rule identifiers and inspect the reasons. Move a satisfactory customized version to Production; the original version changes out of Production according to the supported workflow. This lets you compare behavior before replacing operational output. Do not assume that lowering a threshold always improves security; it may simply increase findings analysts cannot use.

sections.title: Distinguish anomaly generation from correlation
sections.body: An anomaly, a deterministic alert, and a correlated incident are different outputs. Legacy Sentinel Fusion combines suitable signals to recognize multistage attacks and relies on meaningful entities and attack-stage context. For a workspace connected to the Defender portal, use the Defender XDR correlation experience rather than trying to restore Fusion as a separate engine. Wider source deployment can improve visibility, but every contributing source still needs to be configured and healthy. When several low-severity alerts describe the same host and account across stages, investigate the combined story rather than dismissing each alert in isolation.

remember: Tactic is the attacker’s objective; technique is the method.
Available templates do not equal enabled, data-backed detection coverage.
Anomalies describe unusual behavior and require contextual validation.
Customize supported anomaly copies in Flighting before Production.
Fusion is replaced by XDR correlation for Sentinel workspaces onboarded to Defender portal.
pitfalls: A filled ATT&CK cell is not proof of complete protection.
An anomaly does not necessarily create an incident by itself.
Avoid applying old Fusion instructions unchanged to the unified portal.

lab.title: Validate one coverage claim and one anomaly
steps: Select an ATT&CK technique relevant to a training scenario and compare active rules with available templates.
Identify the exact source tables and mappings required by a candidate rule.
Inspect an anomaly’s reasons and baseline-related context.
Review the supported duplicate, Flighting, and Production workflow without changing production content.
lab.done: You can defend a coverage claim with active detection plus data, and distinguish an anomaly from a confirmed attack.

questions.stem: A team points to an available ATT&CK-tagged template as proof that a technique is covered. The template is not active and its data connector is absent. What should the engineer conclude?
options: The technique is fully covered because Microsoft published a template.
Operational coverage is not established until required data and an active validated detection exist.
Adding a tactic label automatically generates the source logs.
The matrix itself blocks the attack technique.
explanations: A content catalog entry is not an operating detection.
Correct. Validate telemetry, activation, scope, and matching behavior before claiming coverage.
Metadata does not configure collection.
The matrix visualizes detection context and does not itself prevent attacks.
questions.takeaway: Coverage claims require evidence-backed active controls.

questions.stem: A built-in anomaly produces excessive benign findings after an application rollout. Choose TWO appropriate engineering actions.
options: Review anomaly reasons and the business change before changing the threshold.
Create the supported customized copy and compare it in Flighting mode.
Assume every anomaly is malicious and isolate all affected hosts.
Overwrite the built-in template directly with an arbitrary query.
explanations: Correct. Context determines whether the finding reflects a threat or a changed baseline.
Correct. Controlled comparison is the supported customization workflow.
Unusual behavior alone is not sufficient proof for a broad response.
Built-in anomaly rules use a defined customization process rather than direct arbitrary replacement.
questions.takeaway: Tune behavioral models with context and comparison.

questions.stem: After connecting Sentinel to the Defender portal, an engineer cannot use Fusion as the previous standalone correlation engine. Which explanation is correct?
options: All correlation is permanently unavailable.
Fusion is disabled for onboarded workspaces and its functionality is replaced by Defender XDR correlation.
A workbook must be renamed Fusion to restore it.
The endpoint agent must be removed to enable incident correlation.
explanations: The unified portal still provides incident correlation through XDR.
Correct. This is a documented platform transition, not necessarily a deployment failure.
A visualization name cannot select a correlation engine.
Removing telemetry would harm visibility and does not restore the legacy engine.
questions.takeaway: Recognize platform changes when interpreting older Sentinel instructions.

questions.stem: Order a controlled customization of a supported built-in Sentinel anomaly rule.
options: Compare results and reasons in Anomalies for the original and customized versions.
Duplicate the supported rule.
Promote the satisfactory customized version to Production.
Modify allowed parameters and enable the copy in Flighting.
explanations: Comparison follows a running test version and supplies evidence for promotion.
Duplication creates the editable supported copy.
Production promotion follows evidence that the change is useful.
Configure and test the copy before replacing production behavior.
questions.takeaway: Duplicate, configure in Flighting, compare, then promote.

title: Custom detections from Advanced Hunting
subtitle: Turn a hunting query into a reliable alert and a precisely scoped response.
intro: A hunting query supports an analyst’s investigation at a chosen moment. A custom detection runs repeatedly to generate alerts and, when configured and supported, response actions. This change creates new engineering obligations: event provenance, entity identifiers, supported frequency, scope, and safe response targeting. Current Microsoft guidance recommends custom detections as the unified rule-creation experience for Defender XDR and Sentinel data in the Defender portal. SC-200 scenarios can ask which fields a summarized query should preserve, why Continuous NRT is unavailable, or why a response cannot act on the intended asset. Design the result schema as carefully as the matching logic.

sections.title: Preserve the source event and asset identity
sections.body: For Defender data, project Timestamp or TimeGenerated so generated alerts retain meaningful event timing. For endpoint tables, keep DeviceId and ReportId for correct device scope and event enrichment. Other Defender sources have their own relevant event and asset identifiers; do not invent a universal DeviceId requirement for email-only data. Keep Timestamp and ReportId from the same real event. If aggregating per device, arg_max can preserve the pair from the latest matching event. Replacing Timestamp with now() or selecting unrelated maximum values can disconnect the alert from the source evidence and damage its investigation context.
sections.code:
DeviceEvents
| where ActionType == "AntivirusDetection"
| summarize Hits=count(), arg_max(Timestamp, ReportId) by DeviceId
| where Hits >= 5

sections.title: Choose frequency from supported query behavior
sections.body: Scheduled custom detections use frequency-dependent lookback behavior; current rules can also use Custom frequency for Sentinel-only data. Continuous NRT evaluates supported events quickly, but the query and selected table must qualify. Current continuous queries use one supported table and supported operators; joins, unions, and externaldata are not supported for that mode. Verify current eligibility rather than assuming every query that runs interactively can run continuously. The service prefilters the rule’s data window, so avoid an arbitrary narrow Timestamp filter that unintentionally removes relevant events. Where extra timing filters are necessary, align them with the intended detection logic.

sections.title: Configure alert content, scope, and action
sections.body: Specify a meaningful alert name, severity, category, and impacted assets. An impacted-asset identifier is also important when selecting supported response actions. Device actions such as isolation act on the returned DeviceId; account, email, and file actions require the corresponding identifiers and source support. Permissions and device-group scope constrain who can create or manage a rule and which devices it can affect. Test a detection without an automatic disruptive action first when the intended result is uncertain. A correct alert on one device should never become an automatic response against a loosely matched display name.

sections.title: Manage the rule as an operational control
sections.body: Run and inspect the hunting query before creating the rule, then review its history, generated alerts, and any configured actions. Investigate rule errors and unexpected volume instead of simply raising severity. Edit, disable, or remove the rule when its purpose changes; document why and verify the resulting coverage. Keep queries efficient by selecting the relevant table, filtering early, and retaining only useful columns after required identifiers are preserved. Treat a rule change as a change to an always-running control: assess scope, event window, benign cases, and action permissions together. A query can be syntactically valid yet operationally unsafe or ineffective.

remember: Preserve real event timing and the relevant source-event identifiers.
For endpoint event enrichment, retain DeviceId and ReportId with event time.
Continuous NRT requires a supported single-table query and supported operators.
Response actions require supported target identifiers and permissions.
pitfalls: Do not replace original event time with now().
Do not aggregate away the identifiers needed for device scope or action targeting.
Interactive hunting success does not prove Continuous NRT eligibility.

lab.title: Convert a harmless hunt into a detection design
steps: Run a harmless official sample query in a training Defender environment.
Inspect which time, event, device, account, or email identifiers it returns.
Add a summarization while preserving a real source event with arg_max.
Check continuous-query eligibility and the scheduled lookback behavior.
Design alert content and an appropriate test scope before enabling any action.
lab.done: You can identify the exact source event and impacted asset from each result row and explain why its frequency is supported.

questions.stem: A DeviceEvents query summarizes five matching events per device. The detection must preserve the latest source event for device-scoped enrichment. Which aggregation is best?
options: summarize Hits=count(), arg_max(Timestamp, ReportId) by DeviceId
summarize Hits=count() by DeviceName | extend Timestamp=now()
summarize max(Timestamp), max(ReportId) by ActionType
project FileName only
explanations: Correct. It preserves DeviceId and takes Timestamp and ReportId together from a real latest matching event.
This loses the stable device identifier and source ReportId, and invents an alert time.
Independent maxima can come from different events and grouping by action loses device scope.
A file-name-only result cannot provide the requested device and event context.
questions.takeaway: Aggregate without destroying source-event provenance.

questions.stem: A custom detection is intended for Continuous NRT. Choose TWO characteristics consistent with current supported query eligibility.
options: It references one supported table.
It uses only supported operators and no joins, unions, or externaldata.
It unions all endpoint and email tables.
It relies on an externaldata lookup downloaded on every evaluation.
explanations: Correct. Continuous custom detections require a qualifying single-table query.
Correct. Supported syntax is narrower than arbitrary interactive hunting.
A union violates the stated continuous-query restriction.
externaldata is not supported for Continuous NRT.
questions.takeaway: Check continuous eligibility before selecting the frequency.

questions.stem: A device custom detection generates the expected alert, but the team wants its supported isolation action to target the exact matched device. Which returned identifier is central to that action?
options: DeviceId
Only a count of affected devices
The analyst’s display name
Only the alert severity label
explanations: Correct. Device actions operate against the identified returned device.
An aggregate count does not identify which device to isolate.
The analyst’s name describes the operator, not the impacted asset.
Severity helps prioritize the alert but does not identify an action target.
questions.takeaway: A response needs an actionable asset identifier.

questions.stem: A rule starts producing far more benign alerts after a query change. What should its owner do?
options: Review the changed query, results, execution history, scope, and actions; tune or disable the rule while correcting the issue.
Increase severity so fewer results exist.
Delete all source events that produced alerts.
Assume a successful save proves the detection is accurate.
explanations: Correct. Manage a detection’s ongoing behavior and any automatic response consequences.
Severity does not reduce the query’s matches.
Deleting evidence is not a sound tuning method.
A saved definition can still be noisy, incorrectly scoped, or inefficient.
questions.takeaway: Operational verification continues after rule creation.

title: Endpoint configuration, device groups, ASR, and custom telemetry
subtitle: Configure protection and collection with precise scope and verified prerequisites.
intro: Endpoint configuration combines several different control planes. Device groups define management scope and remediation levels; endpoint security policies configure protection; advanced features enable additional capabilities; rules configure indicators and other operational behavior; custom collection adds targeted telemetry. SC-200 expects you to choose the right control rather than change a broad setting because it sounds related. A device tag is useful context but is not, by itself, an access-control assignment. A custom collection rule is also different from a custom detection: one gathers selected evidence and the other evaluates evidence to alert. Always identify whether the scenario asks to prevent, collect, detect, authorize, or respond.

sections.title: Use device groups and permissions correctly
sections.body: Device groups match properties such as device name, domain, tags, and operating system, and can assign access to appropriate Microsoft Entra user groups. When a device matches multiple groups, the highest-ranked matching group wins; it does not accumulate every group’s remediation level. Check rank when a critical server receives an unexpected automation setting. Defender XDR unified RBAC controls authorized operations and scope in current deployments; older tenants may expose legacy endpoint RBAC. Tags supply device context for matching and targeting, while roles define what people can do. Do not assume merely tagging a device hides it from all unauthorized readers. The advanced scoped-correlation setting can restrict future correlation to accessible device groups for local SOC operation, but the global SOC may then see multiple incidents instead of one cross-group attack story.

sections.title: Select advanced features and endpoint rule settings
sections.body: Advanced features include capabilities such as live response, EDR in block mode, custom network indicators, tamper protection, device discovery, and product integrations. EDR in block mode can remediate post-breach artifacts when Defender Antivirus is passive; it is not the same as turning on every preventive AV capability. Live response and server live response have feature and permission prerequisites. Indicators under endpoint Rules can define supported allow, warn, or block behavior with scope and expiry. File and network indicator prerequisites differ, so check cloud protection and network-protection requirements. Automation uploads selects extensions for content submission. Automation folder exclusions affect the documented automation/investigation path, can block live-response examination of excluded files, and do not exempt them from antivirus scanning. Treat older AIR-oriented screens in light of the September 2026 lifecycle change.

sections.title: Deploy attack surface reduction as a policy
sections.body: ASR rules target risky behaviors, such as Office spawning child processes, script abuse, or credential theft, rather than only known file hashes. Configure supported policies through Intune or another supported management channel, verify prerequisites for each rule, and test representative devices. Audit records would-be detections without enforcing a block. Block enforces the rule. Warn provides a supported temporary override workflow, with current platform and administrator-approval requirements; not every rule supports it. Review ASR reports and hunting results, use narrow justified exclusions, then expand deployment rings. A global antivirus exclusion is not automatically the correct fix for one ASR compatibility issue.

sections.title: Collect additional evidence with targeted rules
sections.body: Current custom data collection is a preview feature requiring Defender for Endpoint Plan 2, a connected Sentinel workspace, supported endpoint versions, and dynamic tags configured through asset rule management. Static tags are not sufficient for its targeting. Choose the relevant custom event table, actions, and specific conditions, then validate only a small pilot before expanding. Supported custom categories include process, image-load, file, network, and script events in DeviceCustom tables. Collection adds to standard endpoint telemetry instead of replacing it. Sentinel ingestion can incur charges, and event-volume limits apply, so avoid collecting every event unnecessarily. Verify actual rows, DeviceId, rule metadata, and required attributes in the custom table.

remember: The highest-ranked matching device group determines membership.
Tags provide context; RBAC roles and scope grant operations and data access.
ASR Audit observes; Block enforces; Warn has rule and platform limitations.
Custom collection adds evidence and currently requires dynamic tags and a connected Sentinel workspace.
An indicator rule, a collection rule, and a detection rule perform different jobs.
pitfalls: Do not assume every exclusion type applies to every Defender component.
Custom collection preview prerequisites and limits may change; verify before configuring.
Turning on a feature does not give every user permission to invoke it.

lab.title: Plan a small scoped endpoint rollout
steps: Inspect a test device’s tags, matching groups, and group rank.
Identify which role grants a responder the necessary action in the active RBAC model.
Review an ASR rule’s audit results and design a narrow pilot deployment.
Inspect dynamic-tag and connected-workspace prerequisites for custom data collection.
Design a targeted custom collection rule and a query proving that the pilot emitted expected events.
lab.done: You can distinguish protection, collection, detection, and access scope, and validate each against a known pilot device.

questions.stem: A server matches the broad All-Windows group and the more specific Critical-Servers group. It unexpectedly receives the broad group’s remediation level. What should the engineer inspect first?
options: The ranking of the matching device groups.
The color used for the server icon.
Whether a workbook includes the server name.
The size of the server’s incident comments field.
explanations: Correct. A device belongs to the highest-ranked matching group, so specificity alone does not win.
An icon does not determine group membership.
Workbook query results are not the group assignment mechanism.
Incident comment size does not affect endpoint grouping.
questions.takeaway: Device-group priority is explicit ranking, not an assumption of specificity.

questions.stem: A team wants targeted additional script and file telemetry through current custom data collection. Choose TWO prerequisites that directly distinguish this feature.
options: A connected Sentinel workspace for the custom data.
Dynamic device tags configured through asset rule management.
Only a manually assigned static tag.
Only a workbook template and no endpoint deployment.
explanations: Correct. Custom collection routes and queries data through the connected Sentinel workspace.
Correct. Current targeting requires dynamic tags rather than static tags.
Static tags do not meet the documented custom collection targeting requirement.
A workbook neither deploys the endpoint capability nor supplies required telemetry.
questions.takeaway: Custom collection depends on both storage integration and supported dynamic targeting.

questions.stem: An ASR rule may disrupt a legacy line-of-business application. The SOC needs to observe its effect before enforcing it broadly. What is the best initial rollout?
options: Pilot in Audit mode, review ASR reports or hunting data, then move justified rules and exclusions through deployment rings.
Enable Block tenant-wide and ignore compatibility reports.
Turn off all endpoint protection permanently.
Create a file-hash indicator and assume it simulates every ASR behavior.
explanations: Correct. Audit provides evidence about impact before enforcement and a staged rollout limits unintended disruption.
Broad untested enforcement can interrupt legitimate work.
This abandons the protection goal rather than managing compatibility.
Hash indicators and behavior-based ASR rules address different control requirements.
questions.takeaway: Use measured, staged ASR deployment.

questions.stem: An organization uses another primary antivirus and keeps Defender Antivirus passive. It wants Defender endpoint post-breach remediation where supported. Which advanced feature directly fits?
options: EDR in block mode.
Workbook auto-refresh.
A Sentinel Reader assignment.
Disabling every network indicator.
explanations: Correct. EDR in block mode can remediate malicious artifacts detected after breach while Defender Antivirus is passive.
A visualization refresh does not enforce endpoint remediation.
A read-only Azure role does not change endpoint protection behavior.
Removing indicators does not enable the requested protection.
questions.takeaway: Distinguish endpoint post-breach enforcement from the primary antivirus operating mode.

title: Automated response, attack disruption, notifications, and alert tuning
subtitle: Configure response readiness and reduce noise while preserving investigation visibility.
intro: Automation should shorten response time without obscuring what happened. Attack disruption contains high-confidence attacks in progress; action management tracks remediation; notifications route information; alert tuning controls how expected signals appear. These functions are related but not interchangeable. The published SC-200 objectives still name AIR, so learn its remediation-level model and recognize the current lifecycle change: Microsoft states that from September 1, 2026, AIR no longer runs as a separate investigation experience or supports manual triggering; its capabilities run through Defender’s default antivirus protection stack. Older “start AIR investigation” walkthroughs therefore require interpretation rather than literal repetition in an October 2026 tenant.

sections.title: Understand remediation levels and the lifecycle change
sections.body: Full automation allows supported malicious-artifact remediation without a manual approval step; semi-automation introduces approval requirements according to the configured policy, such as core folders or all folders. Device groups are where endpoint remediation levels are associated with intended device populations. Current documentation retains these settings while announcing the retirement of standalone AIR investigation and manual invocation. For on-demand investigation, Microsoft directs operators to a full antivirus scan as needed. Use Action center to review pending decisions and completed action history, verify the relevant permissions, and inspect results. A closed alert does not prove that an expected remediation action succeeded.

sections.title: Prepare for automatic attack disruption
sections.body: Attack disruption uses high-confidence correlated attack signals to contain assets and interrupt lateral movement during an active attack. It is built in rather than a playbook you write for every scenario. Its coverage and actions depend on deployed Defender products and their prerequisites: endpoint onboarding, suitable device discovery, identity sensor auditing and action permissions, or required cloud-app and mailbox configuration. Review device-group automation settings and current exclusions. Semi-automation does not mean every disruption action waits for an operator; current guidance says disruption can trigger without manual approval. Investigate containment in the incident and Action center, then release or restore assets only after assessing the threat.

sections.title: Route the right information to the right people
sections.body: Configure incident email rules for selected severities, sources, and device-group scope. Actions notifications report supported manual or automated response actions, while Threat analytics notifications announce new or updated research reports. Alert email notifications have their own endpoint-oriented configuration. Choose the event type that matches the requirement before adjusting recipients. Notification administration requires suitable settings permissions and respects supported scope. Send a test email, verify delivery filtering, and understand that adding a recipient does not replay all historical events. Current actions notifications do not support custom detections containing response actions, so validate the exact supported notification path.

sections.title: Tune expected signals without broad blind spots
sections.body: Alert tuning can automatically hide, resolve, or, where supported, represent signals as behaviors when precise conditions match expected activity. The available actions vary by source. Hidden endpoint alerts remain available in AlertInfo and AlertEvidence, while behavior output uses its corresponding behavior tables. Built-in tuning has specific exceptions, including custom detections and custom threat intelligence, so do not assume one rule covers every alert family. Correlation groups related signals into an attack story; tuning decides how selected expected signals appear. Use narrow evidence-based conditions, review affected alerts, and preserve visibility for other assets rather than disabling an entire service’s detections.

remember: From Sep 1, 2026, standalone/manual AIR investigation is retired in current Microsoft guidance.
Action center separates pending decisions from completed action history.
Attack disruption is built-in incident-level containment and depends on product prerequisites.
Incidents, actions, threat research reports, and alerts have different notification paths.
Alert tuning actions and exceptions depend on the alert source.
pitfalls: Semi-automation does not universally delay automatic attack disruption.
Receiving email does not establish that remediation completed.
Hiding expected endpoint alerts is not the same as deleting their hunting evidence.

lab.title: Audit response and notification readiness
steps: Read the current AIR lifecycle notice and identify any older lab steps it supersedes.
Inspect a test device group’s remediation level and relevant disruption prerequisites.
Open Action center Pending and History and explain their different purposes.
Draft an incident notification and a Threat analytics notification with appropriate scope.
Review a narrowly scoped alert-tuning rule and identify where its evidence remains searchable.
lab.done: You can explain which component detects, contains, records, notifies, and tunes a scenario, including the current AIR limitation.

questions.stem: An October 2026 training checklist tells an analyst to manually trigger a standalone AIR investigation. Which update aligns with current Microsoft guidance?
options: Standalone AIR and manual triggering were retired from September 1, 2026; use current integrated protection workflows and a full antivirus scan when an on-demand scan is needed.
AIR is now a workbook theme.
All automated endpoint protection was removed with no replacement capabilities.
Manually rename an incident “AIR” to force an investigation.
explanations: Correct. Microsoft distinguishes retirement of that experience from the continued integrated detection and response capabilities.
A workbook display feature is unrelated to the lifecycle change.
The capabilities remain in the default antivirus protection stack.
An incident name is metadata and does not invoke a retired experience.
questions.takeaway: Treat the AIR lifecycle notice as a current-product correction to older labs.

questions.stem: A manager needs notices when high-priority incidents are created and when relevant research reports are updated. Choose TWO notification configurations.
options: Incident email notification rules with the required severity, source, and scope.
Threat analytics notification rules for the relevant reports or tags.
Only an Actions notification rule and no incident or report rules.
A workbook print setting.
explanations: Correct. Incident notifications match the operational incident event.
Correct. Threat analytics notifications match research publication and update events.
Action notifications describe response actions rather than satisfying both requested event types.
Printing does not subscribe recipients to security notifications.
questions.takeaway: Match each notification to the event the recipient actually needs.

questions.stem: A Defender endpoint group uses a supported semi-automation level. The team assumes automatic attack disruption can never contain an active attack without approval. Which assessment is correct?
options: The assumption is too broad; current attack-disruption guidance allows triggering under semi-automation without manual approval, subject to prerequisites and exclusions.
The assumption is always correct for every response action.
Semi-automation disables all sensors.
Device groups control only dashboard colors.
explanations: Correct. Review the specific disruption action and documented configuration rather than applying the artifact-remediation approval model universally.
Different automated response mechanisms have different approval behavior.
Semi-automation is not sensor offboarding.
Device groups influence operational scope and automation settings.
questions.takeaway: Do not generalize one automation approval model to every containment feature.

questions.stem: A narrowly scoped tuning rule uses Hide alert for known benign Defender for Endpoint activity. An investigator later needs to hunt the suppressed evidence. Which statement is accurate?
options: Hidden alerts remain in AlertInfo and AlertEvidence according to current tuning documentation.
Hidden means every corresponding endpoint log is permanently deleted.
Hide alert automatically disables all future endpoint telemetry.
A hidden alert must be restored from a workbook PDF before it can be analyzed.
explanations: Correct. Queue suppression and retained hunting evidence are different concepts.
Hiding an alert is not wholesale deletion of endpoint evidence.
The tuning action does not offboard the device or stop every source event.
A PDF is not required to access retained hunting tables.
questions.takeaway: Understand both the queue effect and the retained evidence of a tuning action.

title: Sentinel automation rules and Logic Apps playbooks
subtitle: Choose the trigger, orchestrate response, and troubleshoot each identity and workflow stage.
intro: A Sentinel automation rule decides when and under what conditions to act; a playbook performs a workflow that can coordinate multiple services. Native automation actions can handle straightforward incident changes, while Logic Apps provide richer enrichment, ticket integration, and response. SC-200 scenarios often include an avoidable mismatch: the wrong trigger, a later rule evaluating a state changed by an earlier rule, a template mistaken for an active workflow, or missing permissions for a service identity. Learn the chain from event to condition to action to authenticated connector. Current Defender case terminology and newer alert triggers also appear alongside legacy Sentinel incident terms.

sections.title: Choose a rule trigger and native action
sections.body: Automation can respond to incident creation, incident updates, or supported alert creation, with available conditions and actions depending on the trigger and portal experience. Use a native action when the requirement is simply assigning an owner, changing severity or status, tagging, or adding a task. A more complex external workflow may call a playbook. Configure narrow conditions and expiration for temporary maintenance or testing exceptions. Rule order matters: later rules evaluate the state left by earlier rules, so a severity change can prevent a later severity condition from matching. Avoid identical priorities when deterministic ordering is required.

sections.title: Build a compatible playbook
sections.body: A playbook is an Azure Logic Apps workflow with a supported Sentinel or Defender trigger and authenticated connector actions. Its trigger must match the event context used by the invoking rule; an incident-trigger automation rule cannot invoke an arbitrary entity-trigger workflow as though it were incident-triggered. Current Defender creation experiences include case and enhanced alert triggers alongside legacy incident, alert, and entity options. Defender may say case while the corresponding Logic Apps connector still says Microsoft Sentinel incident. Install a template when useful, then create and configure an active workflow. For Standard Logic Apps, use a supported stateful workflow and consider network requirements.

sections.title: Authorize execution and connector actions separately
sections.body: The human author needs the appropriate Logic Apps authoring role for the hosting model. Sentinel needs its Automation Contributor permission on the playbook resource group to invoke incident automation. Within the workflow, connector connections act as their configured identity and require appropriate target-system permissions. A managed identity can avoid storing a user password or client secret where supported, but it still needs authorized read or write access to the workspace and any downstream resource. A workflow that starts successfully can still fail on its first API call. Inspect the failing action and identity rather than granting broad permissions to every participant.

sections.title: Test ordering, idempotency, and run history
sections.body: Test manually with harmless data before enabling broad automatic execution. Inspect Logic Apps run history, inputs, outputs, connector responses, and the resulting incident or external record. Make external synchronization idempotent where practical: an incident update should update the existing ticket rather than create duplicates repeatedly. Distinguish rule execution from completion of an external playbook action, and avoid relying on timing that the engine does not guarantee. Review portal-specific update behavior when moving older workflows into the unified experience. Monitor failed or disabled connections, stale credentials, permissions, and changing source fields as part of routine SOC operations.

remember: Automation rule = trigger, conditions, ordered actions; playbook = Logic Apps workflow.
A workflow template must become a configured active playbook before use.
Rule and playbook triggers must be compatible.
Invocation permission and downstream connector authorization are separate.
Later automation rules can see state changes made by earlier ones.
pitfalls: Starting a playbook does not prove all its actions completed.
Automation updates can retrigger workflows; design against loops and duplicate tickets.
Current case terminology can map to incident-named Logic Apps connector operations.

lab.title: Build an enrichment-only automation design
steps: Choose a harmless incident enrichment scenario and document its trigger and conditions.
Create or inspect the compatible workflow with a read-only enrichment action.
Map human, Sentinel service, and connector identity permissions separately.
Run a controlled manual test and inspect every action in run history.
Add a narrow automation rule and validate the resulting incident comment or tag.
lab.done: The expected event starts exactly the intended workflow, and its run history proves the enrichment completed under the correct identity.

questions.stem: The SOC needs all new high-severity incidents from one detection to be assigned to a designated team member and tagged. No external API calls are needed. Which design is most direct?
options: An incident-created automation rule with matching conditions and native assignment/tag actions.
A workbook parameter that changes incident ownership.
A CEF connector that renames owners at ingestion.
An unrelated entity-trigger playbook with no invoking rule.
explanations: Correct. Native rule actions meet the stated simple incident workflow requirement.
Workbook parameters select display/query behavior rather than directly implementing this automation.
Log ingestion is not incident assignment.
An uninvoked incompatible workflow does not implement the required event-based handling.
questions.takeaway: Prefer the simplest supported automation action that satisfies the requirement.

questions.stem: A playbook starts but fails when adding a comment to a Sentinel incident through its managed identity. Choose TWO useful checks.
options: Inspect the failed connector action’s input, output, and authorization error in run history.
Verify the managed identity has an appropriate Sentinel write role, such as Responder, on the target workspace.
Give the human analyst Reader again and assume it changes the managed identity.
Assume successful trigger invocation proves every downstream permission is correct.
explanations: Correct. Action-level diagnostics show where the workflow actually failed.
Correct. The identity performing the write needs the relevant workspace permission.
The human and managed identity are separate security principals.
Invocation and downstream API authorization are distinct checks.
questions.takeaway: Troubleshoot the identity executing the failed action.

questions.stem: Rule A runs first and changes incident severity from High to Low. Rule B runs later and only matches High incidents. What happens when B evaluates the same creation event?
options: B evaluates the updated Low state and does not match that severity condition.
B always sees the original High value regardless of earlier rules.
Both rules must run in parallel.
Rule order only controls the alphabetical display in the portal.
explanations: Correct. Later rules evaluate the current state after preceding rule actions.
That would ignore the documented effect of ordered execution.
Automation rules are sequenced rather than universally parallel.
Order affects execution and therefore can change outcomes.
questions.takeaway: Test automation with the state produced by earlier rules.

questions.stem: An incident-created automation rule cannot select a workflow whose only Sentinel trigger is an entity trigger. What is the best correction?
options: Create or adapt a playbook with a compatible incident/case trigger and configure its required connections and permissions.
Rename the entity-trigger workflow “Incident.”
Increase log retention until the trigger changes.
Save the entity workflow as a workbook.
explanations: Correct. Trigger compatibility is structural and must match the invoking context.
A display name does not change a trigger contract.
Retention does not alter Logic Apps triggers.
A workbook is not an executable response workflow.
questions.takeaway: Match the event contract before debugging workflow logic.
